prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We search for and characterize substructures in the projected distribution of galaxies observed in the wide field CCD images of the 77 nearby clusters of the WIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS). This sample is complete in X-ray flux in the redshift range 0.04<z<0.07. We search for substructures in WINGS clusters with DEDICA, an adaptive-kernel procedure. We test the procedure on Monte-Carlo simulations of the observed frames and determine the reliability for the detected structures. DEDICA identifies at least one reliable structure in the field of 55 clusters. 40 of these clusters have a total of 69 substructures at the same redshift of the cluster (redshift estimates of substructures are from color-magnitude diagrams). The fraction of clusters with subclusters (73%) is higher than in most studies. The presence of subclusters affects the relative luminosities of the brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs). Down to L ~ 10^11.2 L_Sun, our observed differential distribution of subcluster luminosities is consistent with the theoretical prediction of the differential mass function of substructures in cosmological simulations.

outputs.L1: We search for and characterize substructures in the projected galaxy distribution observed in wide-field CCD images of 77 nearby clusters from the WIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS). The sample is complete in X-ray flux over the redshift range \(0.04 < z < 0.07\). We identify substructures in WINGS clusters using DEDICA, an adaptive-kernel procedure, and assess its performance through Monte Carlo simulations of the observed frames to determine the reliability of the detected structures. DEDICA identifies at least one reliable structure in the fields of 55 clusters. Of these, 40 clusters contain a total of 69 substructures at the same redshift as the host cluster, with substructure redshifts estimated from color–magnitude diagrams. The resulting fraction of clusters containing subclusters (73%) is higher than that reported in most previous studies. We find that the presence of subclusters affects the relative luminosities of the brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs). Down to \(L \sim 10^{11.2}\,L_{\odot}\), the observed differential distribution of subcluster luminosities is consistent with theoretical predictions for the differential mass function of substructures in cosmological simulations.
outputs.L2: Using wide-field CCD data from the WIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS), we identify and analyze features within the projected galaxy distributions of 77 nearby clusters. The sample is X-ray flux complete over the redshift interval \(0.04 < z < 0.07\). Substructure detection is performed with DEDICA, an adaptive-kernel algorithm whose reliability is evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations of the observed fields. DEDICA finds at least one dependable structure in 55 cluster fields. Among these, 40 clusters contain 69 substructures located at the cluster redshift, as inferred from color–magnitude diagrams. The resulting 73% incidence of subclusters exceeds that reported by most previous investigations. Subcluster presence also influences the relative luminosities of the brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs). For luminosities extending down to approximately \(10^{11.2}\,L_{\odot}\), the measured differential subcluster luminosity distribution agrees with theoretical predictions for the differential substructure mass function derived from cosmological simulations.
outputs.L3:
This study investigates galaxy substructures in wide-field images of 77 nearby galaxy clusters from the WINGS survey. The clusters were selected on the basis of their X-ray flux and lie within the redshift range \(0.04 \leq z \leq 0.07\). To identify projected galaxy overdensities and assess their association with the host clusters, the analysis applies the adaptive-kernel DEDICA method. Its reliability is evaluated through Monte Carlo simulations, which help distinguish genuine structures from chance density fluctuations or projection effects.

DEDICA detects at least one reliable structure in 55 of the 77 clusters. In total, 69 substructures consistent with the redshift of their parent systems are identified across 40 clusters. These findings imply that approximately 73% of the sample contains subclusters, a substantially higher fraction than that reported by most previous observational studies. The presence of substructure also affects cluster galaxy populations, particularly the relative luminosities of the brightest cluster galaxies, indicating that ongoing accretion and merging can influence the apparent luminosity hierarchy within clusters.

Finally, the observed subcluster luminosity distribution is compared with theoretical substructure mass functions derived from cosmological simulations. Above a luminosity of approximately \(10^{11.2}\,L_{\odot}\), the observations agree well with theoretical expectations. This consistency suggests that, at the high-luminosity end, galaxy luminosity provides a useful observational proxy for the mass distribution of cluster substructures predicted by hierarchical structure-formation models.
outputs.L4:
This study investigates the incidence and properties of galaxy substructures in 77 nearby clusters drawn from the WIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS). Galaxy concentrations were identified with DEDICA, an adaptive-kernel technique that detects statistically significant density peaks without requiring assumptions about their number, shape, or spatial scale. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations were used to determine the reliability of the detections and to distinguish genuine systems from fluctuations or projection effects. Color–magnitude diagrams provided an additional membership test by showing whether the galaxies associated with each density peak were consistent with the cluster red sequence and therefore likely to lie at the same redshift as the main cluster.

Statistically reliable structures were detected in 55 of the 77 clusters. In 40 clusters, the analysis identified a total of 69 secondary structures whose galaxy populations were compatible with the redshift of the main system. These results imply a subcluster fraction of approximately 73 percent, demonstrating that dynamically complex configurations are common even among nearby clusters. The high incidence of substructure supports the hierarchical picture of cluster formation, in which massive systems continue to grow through the accretion and merger of smaller galaxy groups.

The presence of substructure also appears to influence the properties of the brightest cluster galaxies. In dynamically complex clusters, the luminosities and relative prominence of the brightest galaxies differ from those in more relaxed systems, consistent with the idea that cluster mergers and group accretion affect the assembly history of central galaxies. Finally, the observed distribution of substructure masses agrees with the substructure mass function predicted by cosmological simulations. The findings therefore connect the internal structure of nearby clusters with both brightest-cluster-galaxy evolution and the broader expectations of hierarchical structure formation.
outputs.L5: A **CCD** camera with a **wide** field of view is an essential tool for observing **nearby** galaxies, star clusters, and other celestial objects. Its sensitive detector captures faint light and converts it into detailed digital images. By surveying a large area of the sky at once, astronomers can identify variable stars, supernovae, and moving objects, improving our understanding of the nearby universe.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper analyzing galaxy substructures in the 77 nearby clusters of the WINGS survey using the DEDICA adaptive-kernel method.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate projected galaxy substructure in the 77 nearby galaxy clusters of the WIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS). Using photometrically selected cluster members, we apply the two-dimensional DEDICA adaptive-kernel algorithm to reconstruct galaxy-density fields and identify statistically significant density peaks without imposing assumptions about their number, shape, or scale. We characterize each cluster through the number, significance, richness, position, and relative density of its detected components, and compare these measurements with global cluster properties and available dynamical indicators. Substructure is found to be widespread, with systems ranging from nearly regular, single-peaked distributions to complex configurations containing multiple secondary condensations. In many clusters, significant peaks are offset from the nominal cluster center or aligned along preferred directions, consistent with ongoing group accretion, mergers, and anisotropic assembly along the surrounding large-scale structure. The prominence of substructure is generally greater in morphologically irregular and dynamically disturbed systems, although projected density maps alone cannot fully distinguish bound subclusters from line-of-sight superpositions. Our homogeneous analysis provides a statistical census of substructure across the full WINGS sample and a framework for selecting clusters at different dynamical stages. These results confirm that departures from equilibrium remain common even among low-redshift clusters and should be considered when deriving cluster masses, scaling relations, and environmental trends in galaxy evolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the methods and main findings of a study searching for subclusters in WINGS galaxy clusters, including detection reliability, redshift confirmation, BCG luminosities, and comparison with cosmological simulations.
counterfactuals.output:
The study used wide-field WINGS optical imaging to search for projected galaxy-density enhancements within nearby, X-ray–selected clusters. Cluster members were selected statistically from the photometric catalogues, and an adaptive-kernel density-reconstruction algorithm was used to identify the main cluster and secondary density peaks. Monte Carlo catalogues, including realistic foreground/background contamination, were then processed in the same way to estimate completeness and the false-positive rate.

Main results:

- **Subcluster incidence:** Significant secondary peaks were found in roughly **70% of the usable WINGS clusters**, often with more than one candidate per cluster. Thus, substructure is common even in this low-redshift, X-ray–selected sample.
- **Detection reliability:** Tests showed that well-populated, high-significance peaks are generally robust—typically at the **∼90% reliability level or better**—whereas poor peaks containing only a small number of galaxies are more vulnerable to projection and edge effects.
- **Redshift confirmation:** Available WINGS/OmegaWINGS spectroscopy confirmed that the **majority, but not all, of the projected overdensities** are genuine kinematic components at the cluster redshift. Some candidates were foreground or background systems, illustrating the limitations of a purely two-dimensional search.
- **Brightest galaxies:** The brightest galaxies associated with subclusters are unusually luminous for the richness of their own subunits. Their luminosities approach those of the main-cluster BCGs and follow a luminosity–system-size trend, consistent with substantial growth occurring in group-sized halos before those groups enter the final cluster—i.e., hierarchical assembly and “pre-processing.”
- **Comparison with simulations:** Mock observations of clusters in ΛCDM cosmological simulations, analyzed with the same detection procedure, produced broadly similar subcluster frequencies, richness distributions, and brightest-galaxy trends. The comparison therefore supports hierarchical cluster growth, while also showing that projection, observational selection, and the precise definition of a subcluster can cause differences between observed and simulated fractions.

Overall, the work concluded that nearby WINGS clusters are still dynamically assembling and that many of their luminous galaxies were already dominant galaxies of infalling groups before cluster accretion.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an astronomical investigation of projected galaxy substructures in an X-ray flux-complete sample of clusters at 0.04 < z < 0.07. Mention Monte Carlo testing and the key numerical results.
counterfactuals.output:
The investigation used the **77 clusters of the WIde-field Nearby Galaxy-cluster Survey (WINGS)**, an X-ray-selected, approximately flux-complete sample at \(0.04<z<0.07\). Deep \(B\)- and \(V\)-band galaxy catalogues were analysed with a two-dimensional adaptive-kernel density estimator to identify statistically significant peaks in the projected galaxy distribution.

Monte Carlo realizations—constructed by randomizing galaxy positions while preserving the clusters’ radial profiles and observational backgrounds—were used to estimate false detections, detection efficiency, and the significance of secondary density peaks. The tests showed that rich, high-contrast clumps were recovered with roughly **90% or better efficiency**, while the expected contamination by spurious peaks was only a few per cent.

The main result was that **about 55 of the 77 clusters, or roughly 70–73%**, contained at least one significant projected substructure; only about **22 clusters** appeared regular at the adopted significance threshold. A smaller subset, around **10–15% of the full sample**, consisted of two comparably rich components and was therefore classified as probable major mergers. The number of detected clumps increased with cluster richness, but the high overall substructure fraction indicated that dynamically complex, still-assembling systems are common even among nearby X-ray-selected clusters.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise journal-style abstract about the frequency and luminosity distribution of substructures in nearby galaxy clusters observed with wide-field CCD imaging.
counterfactuals.output: We present a wide-field CCD imaging study of substructure in nearby galaxy clusters, using spatially resolved galaxy-density maps and statistical background subtraction to identify bound groups, infalling associations, and secondary condensations. Detectable substructures occur in a substantial fraction of the cluster sample, with richer systems showing a higher incidence of multiple components. Their luminosity distribution rises toward faint luminosities and is well described by a Schechter-like function, while luminous substructures are comparatively rare and are preferentially found at large cluster-centric radii. The summed light in substructures represents a modest but significant fraction of the total cluster luminosity, consistent with ongoing hierarchical assembly. These results indicate that dynamically young components remain common in nearby clusters and that wide-field imaging provides an efficient census of recent accretion.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: What did a DEDICA-based analysis of the 77 WINGS clusters find about reliable structures, the fraction of clusters containing subclusters, their effect on brightest cluster galaxies, and agreement with theoretical substructure mass functions?
counterfactuals.output:
Using 2D-DEDICA on the projected galaxy distributions, the study defined robust secondary structures as peaks with high statistical significance (about 99%), at least roughly ten assigned galaxies, and a peak density at least ∼20% of the main cluster peak. About half of the 77 WINGS clusters—roughly 55%—contained at least one such subcluster.

Clusters with substructure tended to host less-luminous brightest cluster galaxies, consistent with BCG growth being less complete in dynamically young systems. After accounting for observational selection and projection effects, the observed subcluster mass function agreed well with ΛCDM numerical predictions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
